title: China's Nuclear Push Meets Southeast Asia's Trust Deficit
gist: Excerpt of a ThinkChina piece by ASPI CCA researchers: China builds roughly half the world's reactors under construction but has exported reactors only to Pakistan and has no commercial reactor contract in Southeast Asia, where Strait of Hormuz disruptions have revived nuclear interest and Russia, South Korea and others compete on technology, financing and services.

insights.claim: China accounts for roughly half of the world's nuclear reactors currently under construction, yet its overseas reactor exports have succeeded only in Pakistan.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Massive domestic nuclear build capacity has not translated into export wins; watch for the first Chinese reactor deal outside Pakistan as a signal of breakthrough.
insights.quote: China accounts for roughly half of the world’s nuclear reactors currently under construction, but its overseas reactor exports have succeeded only in Pakistan.

insights.claim: Despite Chinese companies' substantial presence in Southeast Asian clean energy industries, Beijing has not yet secured a commercial nuclear reactor construction contract anywhere in Southeast Asia.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Dominance in solar/other clean-energy supply chains does not automatically carry over to nuclear, where trust and long-term ties matter more.
insights.quote: Beijing has yet to secure a commercial reactor construction contract

themes.theme: Hormuz shock reviving SE Asian nuclear demand

insights.claim: Disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz have renewed Southeast Asian governments' interest in nuclear energy as an energy-security option.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Oil/LNG supply shocks are pushing import-dependent Asian economies toward nuclear; a tailwind for reactor vendors, uranium and fuel-cycle services.
insights.quote: Disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz have renewed Southeast Asia’s interest in nuclear energy.
insights.locator: Disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz

insights.claim: Renewed Southeast Asian nuclear interest creates an opening for China to extend its technological and commercial reach in the region.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Watch Chinese state nuclear firms' bids in Southeast Asia as a test of whether they can overcome the regional trust deficit.

insights.claim: Russia, South Korea and other nuclear suppliers are competing with China in Southeast Asia by offering rival technologies, financing arrangements and long-term services.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Financing packages and lifecycle service offers, not just reactor tech, are likely to decide contract awards; Korean and Russian vendors are direct rivals.
insights.quote: Russia, South Korea and other suppliers are offering competing technologies, financing arrangements and long-term services.

insights.claim: Southeast Asian governments' choice of nuclear partners could lock in geopolitical alignments lasting generations, because reactors entail decades-long supplier dependence.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Nuclear vendor selection is a long-duration geopolitical alignment signal; track which suppliers win first contracts in the region.
insights.quote: their choice of partners could carry geopolitical implications lasting generations
